title: Bars and drinks
blurb: Ordering, asking what's good, and getting the round in.

sents.why: 〜をお願いします is the natural way to order. Saying 〜がほしいです is grammatical but blunt.
The counter 二つ follows the noun and its を. Counters never take a particle of their own.

kn: ビールをもういっぱい
sents.why: 一杯 is one glassful; もう in front makes it 'another'.
あります asks whether a thing exists or is in stock. Use います only for living things.
Question words stay in their own block: 何 is the object, so it keeps を.
同じもの literally 'the same thing'. One of the most useful phrases at a bar.
も replaces を entirely when it means 'also'. You never write をも.
弱く is the adverb form of 弱い. Adverbs take no particle, so they sit in the HOW block.
どこ needs no particle before です. You only add で or に when a verb follows.
A fixed expression. No particles, no verb ending — just say it.
Stating the number is enough. 二人です on entering is what staff expect.
〜てください is the standard polite request: verb in て-form plus ください.
Pointing plus これを covers most of a menu you cannot read yet.
An い-adjective plus です is already a complete predicate. Never add だ or another verb.
Potential forms take が, not を. This trips up almost everyone at first.
入っています = 'is in it'. The topic は and the subject が can both appear in one sentence.
お会計 in a restaurant. 勘定 is the older, gruffer word.
別々に is adverbial, so it belongs in the HOW block with no を.
い-adjectives conjugate for past themselves: おいしい becomes おいしかった, then です stays unchanged.
の joins two nouns: 英語のメニュー, an English-language menu.
いくら is a question word, so it keeps its block but drops the particle before です.
の stands in for a noun you have already established — 'a bigger one'.
〜てもいいですか is the standard way to ask permission for anything.
ください after を means 'give me'. After a て-form verb it means 'please do'.
で marks the means. Payment method, transport, tools all use it.
Colour as a noun: 黒 black, 白 white, 赤 red — all usable this way.
The single most reusable sentence pattern in the language: Xはどこですか.
だけ means only. 見ている is the continuous form: currently looking.
Bags are often charged for now, so you will be asked 袋はいりますか.
少し is a bare adverb: no particle, sitting just before what it softens.

title: Trains and directions
blurb: Tickets, platforms, and finding your way.

sents.why: 券売機 is on the sign above the machines themselves.
まで means 'as far as'. 枚 is the counter for flat things: tickets, sheets, plates.
何 plus a counter makes 'which/how many': 何番線, 何時, 何人.
へ is written with the hiragana he but pronounced e. One of only two particles that do this.
終電 — the last train — is worth knowing before you need it.
Drop ます and add たいです to say you want to do something.
から marks the starting point. Pairs naturally with まで.
迷う takes に. Said in the past tense even though you are lost right now.
Show the address to a taxi driver and this sentence does the rest.
The full chain, in order: WHO, TIME, PLACE, HOW, VERB. Every block doing its own job.

title: Hotels and staying over
blurb: Checking in, asking for things, and leaving.

sents.why: が, not は — you are announcing new information rather than commenting on a known topic.
Loanwords take katakana and behave as ordinary nouns.
No に on 何時 here, because です follows rather than a verb.
付いています — 'is attached'. Used for anything that comes with something else.
に marks where something ends up. で would mark where an activity happens.
ません is the polite negative. が because you are reporting a new problem.
Often written Wi-Fi in Latin script on the sign, but said this way.

kn: タオルをもういちまい
sents.why: 枚 again: the counter for flat, thin things.
泊 is the counter for nights of accommodation.
閉まります is the intransitive form: the bath closes. 閉めます would mean someone closes it.
The body part that hurts takes が. Swap in 歯 tooth, お腹 stomach, 足 leg.
Colds are 'pulled' in Japanese: 風邪を引く. A set phrase, not a logical one.
風邪の薬 — medicine of a cold. の does the work an English adjective would.
Worth memorising exactly, swapping in your own allergen, before you travel.
薬局 on the shopfront; ドラッグストア is the larger chain sort.
Point as you say it. が marks the spot that is doing the hurting.
気分が悪い is feeling ill or nauseous, not being in a bad mood.
一日に — 'per day'. に turns a time span into a rate.
呼ぶ is to call someone over. Phoning is 電話します.
もう means 'already/now'. 大丈夫です covers everything from 'I'm fine' to 'no thanks'.

title: Meeting people
blurb: Introductions and the first five minutes of small talk.

sents.why: Said only on a first meeting. Usually followed by よろしくお願いします.
Foreign names go in katakana. 私は is often dropped once it is obvious.
から for origin. イギリス comes from the Portuguese for 'English', not from 'UK'.
The honorific お on 仕事 is because it is the other person's job, not yours.

kn: べんきょうしています
sents.why: 〜ています for something ongoing over a long period, not just this moment.
います for people and animals; あります for objects.
どこ takes で here because an activity happens there. どこに would mark a destination.
The plain present tense covers habits: do you drink, as a rule.
ましょう is 'let's'. 一緒に is a fixed adverb meaning together.

kj: すみません、分かりません
kn: すみません、わかりません
sents.why: 分かりません, not 知りません. The second sounds like refusing to engage.

title: Problems and asking for help
blurb: The sentences you need when something has gone wrong.

sents.why: Gets attention, apologises, and thanks someone. The hardest-working word in Japanese.
度 is the counter for occasions. もう一度 — one more time.
もっと makes any adverb comparative: もっとゆっくり, もっと大きく.
なくす is to lose an object. 道に迷う is to lose your way.

kn: てつだってもらえます
sents.why: 〜てもらえますか is a soft request: could I receive the favour of you doing this.
話せます is the potential form — are you able to. Many speakers say 英語が話せますか with が.
Often more useful than asking someone to repeat themselves.
Softer than it looks in English. Perfectly polite on its own.
The bare て-form, shouted. Emergencies only.
交番 are small neighbourhood police posts, and the standard place to hand in lost property.

title: Time and plans
blurb: Clock times, arrangements, and running late.

sents.why: 今 takes no に. Nor do あした, きょう, まいにち — only specific clock times and dates do.
Here 何時 does take に, because a verb follows rather than です.
は on a time word contrasts it: tomorrow, as opposed to other days.
会う takes に for the person met as well: 友達に会います.
遅れます — I will be late. 遅いです means late in the day, or slow.
空いています — literally 'is open'. Used of schedules, seats and trains alike.
来 means coming: 来週 next week, 来年 next year, 来月 next month.
かかる covers both time taken and money costed.
No verb at all. また plus a time word is a complete goodbye.
Days of the week take に. 曜日 is the same 曜 in every one of them.

title: Work and study
blurb: Your job, your learning, and reading things you cannot yet read.

kn: ロンドンのかいしゃで
sents.why: で because the working happens there. に would just place the company on a map.
Job titles borrowed from English stay in katakana.
始まります — it starts. 始めます would mean someone starts it.
毎日 takes no に, the same as 今 and 明日.
この attaches to a noun; これ stands alone as one.
どう means 'how' and takes no particle, so it sits in the HOW block.
送る covers email, post and seeing someone off.
習う is learning from a teacher; 勉強する is studying under your own steam.
どういう意味ですか — the phrase that unlocks every other phrase.
まだ plus a negative means 'not yet' rather than 'still not'.

title: Home and daily routine
blurb: The shape of an ordinary day.

sents.why: The skeleton sentence: WHO, TIME, VERB. Everything else is an addition to this.
住む always takes に, and always appears as 住んでいます rather than 住みます.
Five blocks, five jobs, in order. で the location of the action, と the person you did it with.
〜の後で means 'after'. The で marks the time frame the action sits inside.
近い measures from somewhere, so it pairs with から.
帰る is specifically to return home or to where you belong. 行く is just going.
が rather than は: you are pointing something out, not commenting on a known topic.
〜ています here is the true present continuous: happening at this moment.
開けます is someone opening it; 開きます is it opening by itself.
朝 as a general time of day takes no に. 朝六時に would.

title: Opinions and feelings
blurb: Liking, disliking, and saying what you think.

sents.why: も replaces は here. You never write 私はも.
好き is an adjective, not a verb, so what you like takes が and never を.
あまり always pairs with a negative ending. On its own it is incomplete.
面白い covers interesting and funny. Context does the separating.
Past tense, because the tiring already happened and you are in its result.
嬉しい is your own feeling. For someone else's you would need 嬉しそうです.
楽しい to 楽しかった. The い-adjective carries the past tense, not the です.
と quotes the thought. Everything before it is what you think.
たい describes your own desire only. For other people, use 行きたがっています.
Agreement, reassurance, or a polite refusal. Tone decides which.
